newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Third Australian team member dies in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Third Australian team member dies in Israel.

text.p: A third member of the Australian team to Israel's Maccabiah "Jewish Olympics" injured in a bridge collapse 12 days ago died overnight, Israeli hospital officials said on Saturday.
Dr Hagai Kedem of Haemek Hospital in the northern Israeli town of Afula confirmed the death of 47-year-old Elizabeth Sawicki, of Melbourne, to Reuters.

Kedem said Sawicki died of lung damage caused by poisons in the water into which the Australian team members plunged as they marched over the bridge towards the stadium on the opening night of the 51-nation Maccabiah Games on July 14.
The bridge over the Yarkon River buckled as competitors from the 370-member Australian team were walking across it.

Two Australians from Sydney -- ten-pin bowler Greg Small, 37, and 50-year-old Yetty Bennet, section manager of the men's bowling team -- were killed and 43 delegation members were injured. Sawicki was on the bridge team.
A spokesman for the Australian contingent to the games demanded on Saturday that Israel compensate families of the deceased and surviving victims.
"Elizabeth's death is a devastating blow to all of the Australian team and once again highlights the magnitude and ongoing effects of the tragedy," Harry Purcel said in a statement.
"Now that the report...has been delivered we call on the government of Israel to swiftly act upon its findings and bring those responsible to justice.
"We implore the government to ensure that immediate compensation is made available to the families of the deceased and to those who have been injured."
An Israeli inquiry into the collapse of the bridge found on Wednesday that faulty design, materials and construction led to the disaster.

The seven-member committee, chaired by the former chief engineer of the Israeli army, submitted its findings to the government, but refrained from recommending any criminal indictments pending completion of a police investigation.
